standing_neutral.description: Adopt an athletic stance that lets you move, pummel, and fight for grips without exposing your neck or balance. Keep posture aligned (head over hips), hands active for hand-fighting, and feet ready for level changes and angle creation. Your first goals are posture, inside position, and distance control—then you can safely enter ties, shoot, or pull guard.
key_concepts: Balanced stance: staggered base, knees soft, weight forward
Posture alignment: head over hips, spine neutral
Hand-fighting: win inside position before big movements
Footwork: step to angles, don’t reach with arms
Level changes: bend at knees/hips, not the waist
Kuzushi: off-balance before entries (snap, pull, circle)
common_mistakes: Head down, exposing neck and posture
Static feet—no angles or level changes

collar_tie.description: Use the collar tie to manage posture and create angles. Control the head with your forearm, keep your elbow down, and combine snaps with footwork to off-balance. Aim to win the inside tie on the other side and connect to takedowns or guard pulls without exposing your neck.
key_concepts: Head control: forearm frames the neck, elbow down
Inside position: win the opposite biceps tie
Snap + step: off-balance then change angle
Posture breaks: head turns, hips follow
Chain attacks: arm drags, knee taps, guard pulls
common_mistakes: Pulling with arms instead of snapping with body
Narrow base while snapping, losing balance

over_under_clinch.description: With one underhook and one overhook, battle to win the inside position and head alignment. Elevate the underhook, whizzer on the overhook, and pummel your feet to angles. Use head position under the chin to steer posture, then connect to throws, trips, or body-lock entries.
key_concepts: Underhook elevation: shoulder-to-shoulder connection
Whizzer pressure: elbow down, shoulder heavy
Head position: under chin, eyes forward
Hip-to-hip connection: deny space
Foot pummeling: step inside to create angles

double_underhooks.description: A dominant clinch. Lock your hands high on the back, clamp ribs with your forearms, keep head inside, and step to angles to lift and move. Prioritize posture before squeezing—your structure creates control. Use body locks, knee pinches, and trips without exposing your neck.
key_concepts: Gable grip behind back—not low at the hips
Rib cage clamp with forearms
Head inside: protect neck, steer posture
Hip lock: step-in angles before lifts
Chain to trips and body lock finishes

single_underhook.description: With one underhook, connect your shoulder to their shoulder and turn them. Keep your head in, elbow deep, and step inside to walk them to an angle. Threaten knee taps and body locks; if they whizzer hard, change levels or re-pummel.
key_concepts: Elbow deep underhook—shoulder connected
Head position protects neck and drives posture
Walk to angles, don’t push straight
Chain entries: knee tap, body lock, re-pummel
common_mistakes: Far hip exposure without head control

closed_guard_bottom.description: Break posture, win grips, and angle your hips before opening. Climb your legs to control shoulders, use two-on-one or collar-sleeve to isolate arms, and connect attacks in chains (sit-up series, pendulum, armbar/triangle/omoplata). Move your hips—not just your arms—to create threats.
key_concepts: Posture control: head/shoulders broken
Hip angle before opening guard
Grip pairs: two-on-one, collar-sleeve
Leg climb: shoulders trapped for attacks
Attack chains: sit-up, pendulum, ATA
common_mistakes: Pulling with arms instead of moving hips

open_guard_bottom.description: Manage distance with frames and hooks, then off-balance before entries. Win inside position with shins and hands, pummel your legs to control the knee line, and use kuzushi (push-pull, angle changes) to create passes or sweep opportunities. Stay mobile—hips lead, feet guide.
key_concepts: Distance management: frames + hooks
Inside position with shins and hands
Leg pummeling to control knee line
Kuzushi before entries: push-pull + angles
Hip mobility drives the guard
common_mistakes: Feet dangling, no hooks or direction

half_guard_bottom.description: Build structure first: knee shield or inside frames to deny crossface and underhook. Win the underhook or frame the far hip, keep head position safe, and connect hip-escape chains to sweeps, reversals, or get-ups. Time your entries when their hands are occupied.
key_concepts: Knee shield / inside frames
Deny crossface; fight for underhook
Far hip frame when no underhook
Elbow-knee connection protects core
Chain: hip escape → sweep/get-up

side_control_bottom.description: Survive and recover: frame the near-side neck/shoulder, frame the far hip, and connect frames to hip escapes. Remove head control first, then re-guard or get to knees. Push with structure, not straight arms, and time movements when top changes base.
key_concepts: Near-side frame at neck/shoulder
Far hip frame denies hip switch
Elbow-knee connection inside
Hip escape chains to re-guard
Timing when top shifts weight

side_control.description: Chest-to-chest control with head and hip management. Crossface to turn the head, block or wedge the far hip, and distribute weight through ribs—not the floor. Use switching bases to isolate the near arm, then progress to knee-on-belly, mount, or submissions.
key_concepts: Crossface: head turned away
Far hip wedge/block to stop hip escapes
Weight through chest and ribs
Switch base to isolate near arm
Progressions: KOB, mount, submissions

mount.description: Stabilize first, then isolate. Use low mount with grapevines or knee ride to settle, then climb to high mount to trap arms and attack. Keep your hips heavy, control the head/shoulders, and connect to s-mount, arm triangles, and back takes as they defend.
key_concepts: Base triangles: hips heavy, hands wide
Low vs high mount progression
Arm isolation: walk hands and knees
S-mount entries and head control
Chains: armbar, triangle, back take

back_control.description: Back control (rear mount) is the apex of jiu‑jitsu positioning. With your chest on their back and your hands controlling the hand fight, you can attack while staying safe. You dictate angles, deny their vision, and force them to defend the choke first. Strong back control isn’t just control — it’s the fastest path to a finish.
key_concepts: Seatbelt hierarchy and hand protection
Hook retention and hip line control
Angle changes: strong/weak side
Head position behind shoulder for choke
Body triangle when control is secured
key_objectives: Keep chest-to-back connection while protecting the choking hand
Win hand fight to expose the neck without losing hooks
Stabilize with seatbelt; switch to strong side when threatened
common_mistakes: Crossing feet on belly—heel hook risk

body_triangle.description: The body triangle turns back control into a locked cage. By fixing their hip line and compressing the ribs, you trade a bit of mobility for crushing control and patient finishing pressure. It slows escapes, elevates the chin, and makes the rear‑naked choke feel inevitable.
key_concepts: Lock behind your knee—not the shin—for security
Hip line isolation limits turning and bridging
Angle toward choking side to expose the neck
Maintain shoulder line above their shoulders
key_objectives: Secure chest-to-back and lock the triangle without crossing feet over the stomach
Turn to the choking side to hide your choking hand and elevate their chin
Use the triangle to slow escapes and set patient strangles
common_mistakes: Shallow lock—triangle slips, giving space (aim for behind the knee)
Locking on the belly—risk of ankle attacks and weak control
Forcing chokes before hand control—gives escapes

seatbelt_straightjacket_top.description: Seatbelt + straightjacket is a back take system built on hand dominance. You trap the defending hand, hide the choking hand, and progress your grips without losing chest‑to‑back. It’s simple, reliable, and designed to turn control into high‑percentage finishes.
key_concepts: Choking arm over; support arm under (seatbelt)
Hand priority: control their top hand first
Use shoulders and head to pin their head line
Progress grips without losing chest-to-back
key_objectives: Trap or control their top hand to free your choking hand
Climb grips to the neck while maintaining hook or triangle control
Finish high-percentage RNC once the chin is lifted
common_mistakes: Attacking with the wrong hand order—your choke gets peeled (control their top hand first)
Separating chest from their back—creates escape space
Reaching over-shoulder without head position—exposes the neck to counters

backpack_latstrap_top.description: The backpack (lat/strap) secures your torso to theirs so your control survives the scramble. By anchoring the chest and managing the hook line, you win the hand fight first, then climb to the neck. It’s a sticky pathway from connection to clean strangles.
key_concepts: Lat/strap grip anchors your torso to theirs
Knee pinch or hooks manage hip line
Head position behind their shoulder for safety
Hand-fight patiently to expose the neck
key_objectives: Stabilize connection with strap grip and maintain hooks
Climb the collar/neck line by removing their top hand
Transition to seatbelt or body triangle once stable
common_mistakes: Loose strap—connection breaks and they turn in
Ignoring knee pinch—feet dangle and hooks slip
Fishing the neck without hand control—wasted attempts

rear_triangle_trap_top.description: The rear triangle trap reduces their defense to one hand and bad hope. By trapping an arm with your legs while staying chest‑to‑back, you increase leverage on the neck and remove most counters. It turns back control into a finishing machine.
key_concepts: Trap an arm with your legs to limit defenses
Angle your body to align the choke
Maintain shoulder line above theirs during adjustment
Use short, tight grips rather than reaching
key_objectives: Isolate one arm and lock the triangle to reduce defense
Angle to the choking side and tighten the shoulder line
Finish with strangles while keeping chest-to-back
common_mistakes: Loose triangle—arm slips free and defense returns
Flattening out—loses angle and choke pressure
Reaching long—breaks posture and gives space

rear_mount_bottom.description: Bottom of rear mount is all about survival and smart exits. Protect the choking hand, turn to the safe side, and put your back to the mat to shed hooks. The goal isn’t to win the position — it’s to break chest‑to‑back, face them, and get back to guards you can fight from.
key_concepts: Two-on-one on choking hand before anything else
Head position down and tucked inside their shoulder
Slide to the safe side (overhook side) to remove hooks
Put your back to the mat to shed chest-to-back
key_objectives: Control and peel the choking hand with two-on-one
Turn to the safe side and lower shoulder line to the mat
Clear one hook at a time and rotate into guard or half guard
common_mistakes: Fighting the wrong hand—choke sinks (always address the choking hand first)
Rolling to the choking side—tightens the strangle and traps your arm
Bridging without hand control—gives neck exposure

body_triangle_escape_bottom.description: Escaping the body triangle means relieving pressure, protecting your neck, and breaking the lock without panic. Turn toward the lock, create slack, and pry at the right joint. Done correctly, you clear a hook, turn to face them, and re‑enter a guard you can fight from.
key_concepts: Turn to the lock side to relieve pressure
Control choking hand before addressing the lock
Open the lock by prying at the ankle-knee junction
Slide hips down to create slack before turning
key_objectives: Protect your neck with two-on-one before attacking the lock
Turn toward the lock, slide hips down, then wedge the lock open
Clear the bottom hook and rotate to guard or half guard
common_mistakes: Attacking the lock first—gets strangled (neck before legs)
Turning away from the lock—increases compression

straightjacket_defense_bottom.description: Straightjacket defense starts with the right priority: the choking hand. Free the trapped wrist, rotate to the safe side, and slide your shoulders to the mat. The aim isn’t to wrestle from a bad spot — it’s to break their attachment and rebuild your guard.
key_concepts: Identify the choking hand immediately
Free the trapped wrist with hand pummeling
Rotate to safe side to shed hooks and chest-to-back
Use chin and shoulder frames to block grip climbs
key_objectives: Break the straightjacket trap while protecting the neck
Turn to the safe side and slide shoulders to the mat
Clear hooks and face them into guard or half guard
common_mistakes: Trying to sit up—exposes the neck
Turning to choking side—gets flattened and trapped

rear_mount_granby_chain_bottom.description: The granby chain is a shoulder‑roll escape that clears hooks and turns you to face the fight. Protect the neck first, then roll toward the safe side to break chest‑to‑back. If you keep moving, you’ll recover guard before they can re‑attach.
key_concepts: Neck safety first, movement second
Roll toward the safe side to clear hooks
Chase shoulder-to-mat to break chest-to-back
Face the hips to recover guard
key_objectives: Two-on-one the choking hand, then granby toward safe side
Clear the bottom hook during roll and face their hips
Establish guard or half guard on the turn
common_mistakes: Rolling without hand control—neck gets exposed

rear_mount_inversion_bottom.description: Inversion from back control is a last‑resort space maker. When standard escapes are blocked and your neck is safe, invert to free a hook and turn to face their hips. It’s not about flair — it’s about making enough room to rebuild guard and get back to work.
key_concepts: Use inversion selectively when standard escapes fail
Hide neck and elbows tight before inverting
Create space at the hip line before rotating
Re-guard on the turn to prevent re-attachment
key_objectives: Control choking hand, then invert to create hip space
Kick free a hook and turn to face their hips
Recover guard before they reconnect
common_mistakes: Inverting to the choking side—tightens control

high_mount_top.description: High Mount Control is a control platform that turns pressure into progress. With gravity, balance, and leverage on your side, you can isolate limbs, climb to chokes, or transition to even stronger control. The person underneath burns energy and runs out of safe options — strong control here isn’t just stability, it’s a path to the finish.
